newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan president demands anti-corruption drive.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan president demands anti-corruption drive.

text.p: Pakistani President Farooq Leghari urged Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's government and the opposition on Monday to cooperate in setting up parliamentary committees to tackle what he called the disease of corruption.
"I feel the time for action has come," Leghari said in a letter to both houses of parliament.
He recalled his own past appeals to the government to "strengthen efforts to root out corruption at all levels as this disease is eroding our moral and social fabric".
Parliamentary sources said the letter, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, was expected to be read in the National Assembly (lower house) late on Monday night.
Leghari said Bhutto and main opposition leader Nawaz Sharif had both welcomed in July his proposal for parliamentary select committees to combat corruption, but no progress had been made.
Sharif had earlier demanded a permanent judicial commission to probe corruption charges against government politicians and bureaucrats. Bhutto had said existing mechanisms were adequate.
Leghari proposed several changes to existing legislation, including an amendment to bar those found guilty of misconduct from public office for seven years.
His action was a rare step into the political fray for a president who has kept a low profile since he was elected after Bhutto came to power in October 1993.

But it was the second time in three days that Leghari, once seen as a faithful political ally of Bhutto, had taken an independent initiative. On Saturday, he aired his differences with the prime minister over the issue of judicial appointments.
Under Pakistan's constitution, the president has the power to dismiss an elected government and dissolve parliament.
Leghari has in the past advocated scrapping these powers, used several times by his predecessors, as an inappropriate legacy of former military ruler General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq.
